source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: Atypicality (A-index, Uzzi 2013 z-scores on journal pairs) and disruption (D-index, Funk and Owen-Smith) capture distinct processes. Atypical work extends known concepts into new topics. Disruptive work replaces a dominant idea inside its own topic.
numbers: 41 million articles 1965-2024 (OpenAlex, 49M corpus); figure analyses use 40,453,825 (1965-2020) and 40,935,251 articles. Top 5% cutoffs: D > 0.04, A > 22.9.
quote: Disruption, in contrast, signifies the replacement of a dominant idea within its own topic.
limits: Full PDF text read, but equations, correlation coefficients and tables are not in the text layer; only binned figures. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Open mode should treat distant combination and replacing the leading rule as two move types with different payoffs.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas? (H1 result)
finding: H1 supported: across disciplines, time periods and team sizes, papers with higher A-index have lower mean D-index. Authors read this as recombination and displacement being separate pathways.
numbers: Binned mean D by A bin, 95% bootstrap CIs; N = 40,935,251 articles; strata: discipline, period, team size. No single r in the text.
limits: Correlational. Seems to conflict with Lin, Evans, Wu 2022 (c05: high atypicality almost twice as likely to disrupt); different units (tail probability vs mean D) may explain it.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that rewards only far-analogy novelty will not produce rule replacement. Keep a separate attack-the-incumbent operator.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas? (LLM use 1: theory vs method)
finding: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, zero-shot, labelled each highly cited disruptive paper against its most-cited reference as theory innovation (conceptually different) or method innovation (refinement). Probability of theory falls as the year gap to the reference grows: conceptual advances come soon after their reference, formal refinements later.
numbers: 50,147 papers with D>0; 52,488 highly cited papers 1900-2020 in Fig 4; token probability of option 1 used as score. Robust to few-shot examples (Turing-Church, Watts-Milgram), reworded options (conceptual vs formalism difference) and a third others option.
limits: No human validation accuracy for the LLM labels in the text. Single model. Probability is not calibrated truth.
agent_relevance: Cheap pattern: ask a model to compare a new item with its closest precedent and classify replace vs refine. Usable as a move classifier in the loop.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas? (LLM use 2: topical similarity)
finding: Introduction says an LLM computed topical similarity between each paper and its most-cited reference. Disruptive papers show strong topical correspondence with that reference; atypical papers show low similarity to dominant references. This is the structural test of functional equivalence.
numbers: Holds after controlling for field, citation counts and time. No coefficient in the extracted text.
limits: Only the claim was recoverable; results table not in the text layer. Size unknown.
agent_relevance: A displacing move must target the same job as the incumbent. Check 'does my candidate do the same job better' is an LLM comparison.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New Directions in Science Emerge from Disconnection and Discord (J. Informetrics)
finding: Abstract: papers with high atypicality are almost twice as likely to disrupt science as conventional papers. Disruption can take ten years or more to stabilise. First model treating atypicality as distance between latent knowledge spaces learned by neural networks.
numbers: almost twice as likely (abstract only); ten-plus years to stable D.
limits: Abstract page only. Direction differs from the 2025 result; needs full text to reconcile.
agent_relevance: Early signal of a good idea may be atypicality, but disruption shows only after years. A short loop can only proxy it.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2024) Displacing Science (arXiv 2402.16839, withdrawn)
finding: Eight-year investigation: interviews across nine disciplines plus 41 million papers over six decades. Confirms decline in disruptive papers. Reads the D as Displacing. Proposes a principle of functional equivalence: not all innovation problems are combinatorial. Challenges the view that AI is the mature solution to scientific innovation. Says NIH and NSF are less likely to fund disruptive work.
numbers: 41 million papers; 9 disciplines (interviews); 6 decades.
limits: Withdrawn by the authors (v9) to split into separate papers; claims not final.
agent_relevance: Warns against assuming a recombination engine (a language model remixing known text) will displace anything.

source: Fang and Evans (2025) Generalization and the Rise of System-level Creativity in Science
finding: Citation analysis separates foundations, extensions and generalizations. Foundations and extensions dominated post-war and declined after the 1990s. Generalizations (reused across many fields) rose sharply. Argues the disruption index conflates modes, so the decline reading is overstated; links the shift to the Internet and LLMs.
numbers: Tens of millions of publications (OpenAlex, Web of Science); 134 pages, 79 figures. No index values on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only. A competing explanation of the D-index decline.
agent_relevance: Competing metric to D. Selection should not rely on one novelty number.

source: Wang (2024) A Content-Based Novelty Measure for Scholarly Publications: A Proof of Concept
finding: Treats novelty as atypical combination, measured as the surprise a language model assigns to the word distribution of scholarly text. Checked for face validity and for construct validity against a panel of domain experts.
numbers: No figures on abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only. Single author, proof of concept (iConference 2024).
agent_relevance: Language-model surprisal is a text-only stand-in for Uzzi atypicality; needs no citation graph, so an agent can compute it now.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review: LLM-agent ideas rated more novel than expert human ideas; feasibility slightly lower. A human rerank raised novelty further.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition (human, AI, AI+human rerank); 79 reviewers; 298 reviews. Novelty per review: human 4.84 (SD 1.79, n=119), AI 5.64 (n=109, p<0.01), AI+rerank 5.81 (p<0.001). Per idea: 4.86 vs 5.62 (p=0.03) vs 5.78 (p<0.01). Feasibility 6.34 vs 6.61, not significant.
limits: Novelty judged by people at idea stage, not by outcome. NLP prompting-style topics only.
agent_relevance: LLM ideas win on perceived novelty (the distant-combination feel); see c11 and c12 for what happens after execution.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) same paper: duplication and self-evaluation
finding: Agent made 4,000 seed ideas per topic but only about 200 were non-duplicates (5%) at cosine 0.8. LLM judges rank ideas near chance.
numbers: Best LLM evaluator 53.3% pairwise (Claude-3.5), others 43.3-51.7%, chance 50%; human inter-reviewer agreement 56.1% (NeurIPS 2021 66.0%, ICLR 2024 71.9%).
limits: First 100k characters of the page read; remainder not read.
agent_relevance: Over-generate-and-rank fails twice: duplicates shrink the pool and the ranker is near chance. Selection needs outside signals.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: Experts executed randomly assigned LLM or human ideas. After execution, LLM ideas lost significantly more score than human ideas on novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall.
numbers: 43 experts, over 100 hours each, 4-page paper each; larger drop for LLM ideas, p<0.05 on all four metrics.
limits: Abstract page only; exact means not seen.
agent_relevance: Novel-sounding combinations lose value once tested. Select after cheap execution, not at idea stage.

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research (ACL 2025)
finding: Experts checked AI-generated research documents for hidden borrowing. Many novel-looking ideas map one-to-one onto earlier work without citation, and plagiarism detectors miss it.
numbers: 13 experts, 50 documents; 24% paraphrased with one-to-one method mapping or substantially borrowed; 76% some overlap; only a small fraction fully novel.
limits: Documents from specific idea-generation systems; newer models may differ.
agent_relevance: A surface-word atypicality score is fooled by paraphrase. Check structural mapping to prior art.

source: RQ-Bench authors (2026) On the Limits of LLM-as-Judge for Scientific Novelty Assessment
finding: LLM judges, standalone and comparative, rated model-generated research questions as highly novel (a novelty mirage). Comparison made it stronger. Domain experts preferred the author-anchored reference questions. Many generated questions were narrow and tied to the source.
numbers: No numbers on abstract page.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Do not let a model judge its own novelty. Use external anchors.

source: Are We Truly Innovating? Originality in AI Research Papers (2026)
finding: Analysis of peer-review text on originality. LLM agents asked to assess originality overestimated novelty and struggled to detect paraphrased conceptual plagiarism.
numbers: More than 100,000 peer-review reports from leading AI venues.
limits: Abstract only; no accuracy numbers.
agent_relevance: Second study with the same bias: LLM novelty ratings are inflated.

source: SchNovel (2024) Evaluating and Enhancing LLMs for Novelty Assessment in Scholarly Publications
finding: Benchmark of paper pairs where the more recent paper is assumed more novel. RAG-Novelty, which retrieves similar papers first, beats baselines.
numbers: 15,000 pairs, six fields, arXiv, publication dates 2 to 10 years apart.
limits: Label assumption (newer = more novel) is crude. No scores on abstract page.
agent_relevance: Retrieving nearest precedents before judging novelty helps. A cheap scaffold step.

source: NovBench (2026) Evaluating LLMs on Academic Paper Novelty Assessment
finding: Models writing novelty evaluations were scored on Relevance, Correctness, Coverage, Clarity. General and specialised models under various prompting strategies showed limited grasp of novelty; fine-tuned ones often failed to follow instructions.
numbers: 1,684 paper-review pairs from an NLP conference.
limits: Abstract only; no scores.
agent_relevance: Prompting alone did not fix novelty judgment.

source: Automated Novelty Evaluation of Academic Paper: A Collaborative Approach Integrating Human and LLM Knowledge (2025)
finding: Argues expert judgment is limited by reviewer knowledge and that counting unique reference combinations (Uzzi style) is an uncertain proxy. Combines LLM summaries of method sections with novelty sentences from peer reviews to fine-tune BERT with a sparse-attention fusion module.
numbers: No numbers on abstract page; claims to beat many baselines.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Hybrid: combine the reference-combination signal with text understanding.

source: Huang (2026) Catalyst Papers in AI Research: A Landscape on ICLR 2017-2025
finding: Compared four disruptiveness measures for finding papers that redirect later research. An LLM-based semantic rater did worst, below chance. Peer-review scores did not predict future disruptiveness.
numbers: 36,113 ICLR papers. AUC for highly cited: EDM 0.83, CD index 0.60, node2vec 0.49, LLM rater 0.42. Topic initiators 7.55x topic-share growth; topic bridges 11.52x cross-topic flow. Review score vs disruptiveness |rho| <= 0.005; accepted vs rejected EDM p=0.11.
limits: AI-conference papers only; abstract page only.
agent_relevance: A text-only LLM rating of 'will this replace the leader' was worse than a coin. Do not use it. Separate bridges (atypical) from initiators.

source: Semantic Geometry for Uncovering Paradigm Dynamics via Scientific Publications (2026)
finding: R-P-C framework (references, paper, citing papers) in semantic space. Atypical reference combinations are an upstream disturbance that can trigger a semantic rupture; disruption rests on distance between a paper's knowledge base and its diffusion. Small teams explore more; large teams consolidate. Consolidating work is recognised fast; exploratory work diffuses slowly and selectively.
numbers: No numbers on abstract page. 40 pages, 17 figures.
limits: Abstract only. Links the two metrics causally, unlike the 2025 negative-correlation paper.
agent_relevance: Embedding geometry lets an agent compute atypicality-like and disruption-like quantities for its own candidates.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Identifying Disruptive Models in the Open-Source LLM Community
finding: Model Disruption Index (MDI) applies the disruption idea to model lineage on Hugging Face. Most models are consolidative. Disruptive positions are more common among large models and finetuned ones.
limits: Abstract only; formula not seen.
agent_relevance: D-index logic transfers to AI artifacts: a new item is disruptive if later work cites it instead of its parents.

source: Nova (2024) Iterative Planning and Search to Enhance Novelty and Diversity of LLM Generated Ideas
finding: Plan-then-retrieve loop pulls outside knowledge step by step into idea generation. Yields more unique novel ideas.
numbers: 170 seed papers; 3.4x more unique novel ideas; at least 2.5x more top-rated ideas than prior best (Swiss tournament).
limits: Abstract only; evaluation partly automated.
agent_relevance: Retrieving more distant knowledge then regenerating raises distinctness: an atypicality-seeking scaffold.

source: Tracing the Influence of Retrieved Literature on Scientific Ideation in LLMs (2026)
finding: Five retrieval strategies vs a no-literature baseline. Within one paper set, retrieval reduced idea diversity; pooling across paper sets raised it. In most ideas one or two papers dominate.
numbers: 45,000 ideas, 15 ML topics, 10 open-weight models. Within-set diversity -5.6% to -17.9%; pooled +10.2% to +18.1%; 79.3% of ideas dominated by 1-2 papers; attribution spread vs diversity r=0.70.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Retrieval alone anchors on few sources. For atypical combination, feed distant and varied source sets.

source: Heuresis (2026) Search Strategies for Autonomous AI Research Agents Across Quality, Diversity and Novelty
finding: Six search strategies (greedy, MAP-Elites, Go-Explore, Islands, Curiosity, Omni) steer where ideas land but do not widen the quality-novelty frontier. Novel ideas never reach the top quality of known recipes.
numbers: 3,222 scored runs, 3 domains. None rated Original. One novel idea in the top 10 by quality across all strategies. 40 confirmed fabrications in 1,628 runs (reward hacking).
limits: Abstract only; ML domain.
agent_relevance: Keep atypical branches in a separate lane with their own acceptance bar, and audit for fabrication.

source: Multi-agent AI systems outperform human teams in creativity (2026)
finding: Multi-agent LLM teams beat human teams on creativity; novelty drove the gain. Wide-ranging discussion (low global coherence) predicted creative ideas in both. Model choice and discussion structure were separate levers.
numbers: 4,541 LLM-team ideas vs 341 human ideas, six tasks, Cohen's d=1.50; the two levers explained 26.8% of variance in conversational dynamics.
limits: Abstract only; creativity rated on novelty and usefulness, not displacement.
agent_relevance: Semantic spread of a discussion can be measured with embeddings and used as a control knob.

source: Cooking Up Creativity: Enhancing LLM Creativity through Structured Recombination (DishCOVER) (2025)
finding: LLM translates recipes to structured representations, applies cognitively inspired manipulations (recombination), then translates back. Claimed to beat GPT-4o on novelty and diversity.
numbers: No numbers on abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; recipe domain.
agent_relevance: Structured recombination operators beat free prompting; relevant to operator design.

source: Enhancing Research Idea Generation through Combinatorial Innovation and Multi-Agent Iterative Search (2026)
finding: Multi-agent generate-evaluate-refine loop with iterative knowledge search inspired by combinatorial innovation theory. Claims better diversity and novelty in NLP; quality lies between accepted and rejected top-venue papers.
numbers: No numbers on abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Uses recombination theory only.
agent_relevance: Agent literature builds recombination; displacement-style moves are missing.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology (Nature 566)
finding: Cited by Li et al. 2025 as the source of the validated D-index method; small teams disrupt, large teams develop. Not read first-hand.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Second-hand citation only.
agent_relevance: Team-size effect may matter for multi-agent design.
